title: Arguments, Environment, Time and Processes
intro: Talking to the world outside your program: command-line arguments and environment variables (`std::env`), measuring time (`std::time`), and running other programs (`std::process`).

coming_from.go: `env::args()` is `os.Args`, program name first. `Instant` is the monotonic reading that a `time.Time` from `time.Now()` carries (`time.Since`), and `Command` is `exec.Command`. Go has a `flag` package in its standard library; Rust's has no flag parser (the `clap` crate does that). `env::var` returns a `Result`, where `os.Getenv` returns an empty string.
coming_from.kotlin: `env::var` is `System.getenv`, with a `Result` instead of a platform-type `String!` that may be `null`. Kotlin's `main` can take `args` without the program name, while `env::args()` has it first. `Instant` is `TimeSource.Monotonic` (or `System.nanoTime`), and `Command` is `ProcessBuilder`.
coming_from.python: `env::args()` is `sys.argv`, program first. `env::var` returns a `Result`, where `os.environ.get` gives `None` and `os.environ[...]` raises `KeyError`. `Instant` is `time.monotonic`, `SystemTime` is `time.time`, and `Command` is `subprocess.run`.
coming_from.typescript: `process.argv` starts with `node` and then your script; `env::args()` starts at your program, so `argv.slice(2)` is `args().skip(1)`. `env::var` returns a `Result` instead of `string | undefined`. `Instant` is `performance.now()`, `Command` is `child_process.spawnSync`, and `thread::sleep` blocks its thread.
coming_from.java: `env::var` returns a `Result` instead of `null`. Java's `main(String[] args)` leaves out the program name; `env::args()` has it first. `Instant` is `System.nanoTime()`, not `java.time.Instant` (that one is wall-clock time, Rust's `SystemTime`). `Command` is `ProcessBuilder`.
coming_from.csharp: `env::var` returns a `Result`, where `GetEnvironmentVariable` returns `null`. The `args` of `Main` leave out the program name; `Environment.GetCommandLineArgs()` has it first, like `env::args()`. `Instant` is `Stopwatch`, `SystemTime` is `DateTime.UtcNow`, and `Command` is `Process` with `ProcessStartInfo`.
coming_from.c: `env::args()` is `argv`, program name first, and `env::var` is `getenv` with a `Result` instead of `NULL`. `Instant` is `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` on Linux. `Command` starts the program directly with separate arguments; `system` and `popen` hand one string to `/bin/sh`.
coming_from.cpp: `Instant` is `std::chrono::steady_clock` and `SystemTime` is `system_clock`. `env::var` is `std::getenv` with a `Result` instead of `nullptr`. The C++ standard library can only run a program through `std::system`, which hands a string to the shell; Rust's `Command` starts it directly, one argument at a time.

notes: `env::args()` includes the program name first, like `argv` in C, `sys.argv` in Python and `os.Args` in Go. Java, Kotlin and C# `main` arrays leave it out. The standard library does not parse flags: the [`clap` guide](/build/clap/) does.

`env::var` returns `Result<String, VarError>`, so "unset" is an error you can see, separate from "set to empty". In many languages a missing variable comes back as an empty string or null, and nothing makes you check. The gotcha below shows where that bites.

`Instant` is for measuring: the docs call it a clock that is "monotonically nondecreasing", so setting the system clock does not move it. `SystemTime` is wall-clock time, for timestamps, and can go backwards. Neither knows about dates or time zones: for those you need a crate such as `jiff`, `chrono` or `time`.

`Command` doesn't go through a shell. `Command::new("ls -la")` looks for a program literally named `ls -la`. Pass each argument separately with `.arg()`. `.output()` waits and captures, `.status()` waits and lets the child print straight to your terminal, and `.spawn()` starts it and lets you carry on.

What a program prints is bytes, not a `String`: `String::from_utf8_lossy` turns the bytes into text and replaces anything that isn't valid UTF-8. `std::process::exit(1)` stops the program right away and skips cleanup (destructors don't run), so returning from `main` is usually nicer.

gotcha.title: Using an environment variable as if it's always set
gotcha.looks_fine: `os.Getenv("RBC_PORT")` gives back a string. If you forgot to set it, you get an empty string, the program carries on, and it prints `listening on port` with nothing after it.
gotcha.rust_sees: `env::var` returns a `Result`, because the variable might be missing or not valid UTF-8. A `Result` can't be printed with `{}`, so you have to decide what missing means.
gotcha.why: Run the versions in other languages: seven of them run and print a blank, `null`, `None`, `undefined` or `(null)` where the port should be, and C++ aborts. That is the classic bug that works on a machine where the variable is set and fails in a container where it is not. In Rust you choose on purpose: a default with `unwrap_or_else`, or a clear error with `?` or `expect`.

go.says: Go prints `listening on port ` with nothing after it. An unset variable comes back as an empty string, with no error.

kotlin.says: Kotlin prints `listening on port null`. `System.getenv` is a Java method, so Kotlin sees its result as a platform type `String!`: nothing makes you check for null, and adding it to a string turns null into the text "null". `port.length` would throw a NullPointerException instead.

python.says: Python prints `listening on port None`. `os.getenv` returns None for a missing variable, and it prints happily. Writing `os.environ["RBC_PORT"]` instead would crash with a KeyError.
python.code:
import os

port = os.getenv("RBC_PORT")
print("listening on port", port)

typescript.says: Prints `listening on port undefined`. `process.env.RBC_PORT` is typed `string | undefined`, but `console.log` takes anything, so TypeScript lets the missing value through.
typescript.code:
const port = process.env.RBC_PORT;
console.log("listening on port", port);

java.says: `getenv` returns null for a missing variable, and string concatenation turns it into the text "null". It runs fine and prints `listening on port null`, just like Kotlin.

csharp.says: `GetEnvironmentVariable` returns null for a missing variable, and string interpolation prints null as nothing. It runs and prints `listening on port` with an empty port, the same bug as Go.

c.says: `getenv` returns NULL for a missing variable, and passing NULL to `%s` is undefined behaviour. glibc happens to print `listening on port (null)`; other C libraries can crash, and gcc doesn't warn.

cpp.says: `std::getenv` returns nullptr for a missing variable, and building a `std::string` from it is undefined behaviour. libstdc++ catches it and throws `std::logic_error`, so the program aborts before printing anything.

kotlin.code:
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    println("${args.size} arg(s) after the program name")

    val port = System.getenv("RBC_PORT") ?: "8080"
    println("port $port")
    val missing = System.getenv("RBC_MISSING")
    println(if (missing != null) "RBC_MISSING=$missing" else "RBC_MISSING: not set")

    val start = System.nanoTime()
    Thread.sleep(20)
    val tookMs = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000
    println("slept at least 20ms: ${tookMs >= 20}")

    val p = ProcessBuilder("echo", "hello from echo").start()
    print(p.inputStream.bufferedReader().readText())
    println("exit ok: ${p.waitFor() == 0}")
}

python.code:
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time

# argv: the first one is the script itself
print(f"{len(sys.argv) - 1} arg(s) after the program name")

# environ.get returns None (or your default) when the variable isn't set
port = os.environ.get("RBC_PORT", "8080")
print(f"port {port}")
missing = os.environ.get("RBC_MISSING")
print(f"RBC_MISSING={missing}" if missing is not None else "RBC_MISSING: not set")

# monotonic clock for measuring, in nanoseconds
start = time.monotonic_ns()
time.sleep(0.020)
took_ms = (time.monotonic_ns() - start) / 1_000_000
print(f"slept at least 20ms: {took_ms >= 20}")

# run another program and capture what it prints
out = subprocess.run(["echo", "hello from echo"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(out.stdout, end="")
print(f"exit ok: {out.returncode == 0}")

procs.py.code:
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from datetime import timedelta

print("len(sys.argv):", len(sys.argv), "(the script name is argv[0])")

# a list of arguments: no shell; a failing program is a return code unless check=True
out = subprocess.run(["echo", "a  b", "$HOME", "one; echo two"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("output:", repr(out.stdout))
print("false returncode:", subprocess.run(["false"]).returncode)
try:
    subprocess.run(["false"], check=True)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print("check=True raises:", e)

# input= is written to the child's stdin and the pipe is closed for you
sorted_out = subprocess.run(["sort"], input="pear\napple\n", capture_output=True, text=True)
print("sort printed:", repr(sorted_out.stdout))

# a missing variable
try:
    os.environ["RBC_MISSING"]
except KeyError as e:
    print("os.environ[...] raises KeyError:", e)
print("os.environ.get:", os.environ.get("RBC_MISSING"))

# monotonic vs wall clock; a timedelta is signed
start = time.monotonic()
time.sleep(0.02)
print("monotonic elapsed >= 20ms:", time.monotonic() - start >= 0.02)
print("1s - 2s:", timedelta(seconds=1) - timedelta(seconds=2))

# sys.exit raises SystemExit, so finally and with blocks still run; os._exit does not
for call in ["sys.exit(0)", "os._exit(0)"]:
    code = f"import os, sys\ntry:\n    print('calling {call}')\n    {call}\nfinally:\n    print('finally ran')"
    print(subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", code], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout, end="")

timeout.py.code:
import subprocess

# timeout=: when it passes, subprocess.run kills the child and raises
try:
    subprocess.run(["sleep", "60"], timeout=0.2)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as e:
    print("TimeoutExpired:", e)

# a child ended by a signal has a negative returncode
print("kill -9 returncode:", subprocess.run(["sh", "-c", "kill -9 $$"]).returncode)
